items.title: Stimulation uncertainty reveals distinct mechanisms of sensation seeking and impulsivity
items.author: Charley M. Wu
items.content: Classical accounts of sensation seeking emphasise attraction to stimulating outcomes. This study examines the complementary role of uncertainty, showing that sensation seekers seek uncertainty when stimulation value is low but avoid it when value is high, a profile distinct from impulsivity.

items.title: Effect sizes for brain-based predictive models of cognition across the lifespan
items.author: E. Dhamala
items.content: This review synthesizes literature on brain-based cognitive predictions using large-scale datasets, examining how methodological choices and data-related factors impact model performance. Key advances are proposed to improve the precision and utility of brain-based cognitive predictions.

items.title: Young children prefer to learn from and befriend strivers rather than endowed individuals
items.author: Kathleen H. Corriveau
items.content: Across two studies, 5- to 9-year-old children selected between a striver and an endowed informant when making epistemic and social decisions. This study found that children preferred the striver as a source of information and social partner even when both individuals differed in their outcomes of success.

items.title: Task-specific theta enhancement and domain-general alpha/beta suppression as oscillatory signatures of cognitive flexibility
items.author: Anna-Lena Schubert
items.content: Using time-frequency analysis and latent change structural equation modeling on cued-task switching data, we show that parietal alpha/beta suppression indexes cognitive flexibility with stronger suppression indicating more effective task preparation.

items.title: Little evidence for cultural differences in automatic imitation
items.author: Jan Crusius
items.content: This study investigates whether automatic imitation differs across representative samples from 22 culturally diverse nations. We find no credible evidence for cultural differences, supporting the idea that automatic imitation is a robust and widespread human tendency.
